title: Two Keys
statement: A calculator display shows $1$. The calculator has exactly two keys: one adds $1$ to the displayed number, and the other multiplies the displayed number by $3$. How many different sequences of key presses change the display from $1$ to $30$?
hints: Think about the final key press of a sequence that ends on a number $n$. What could the display have shown just before that press?

Use recursion. Let $f(n)$ be the number of sequences taking the display from $1$ to $n$, then express $f(n)$ using the values of $f$ at the smaller numbers from which $n$ can be reached in one press. These are $n-1$ and, when $3$ divides $n$, also $\frac{n}{3}$.

With $f(n)$ as the number of sequences from $1$ to $n$, we have $f(1)=1$, and for $n \ge 2$ we have $f(n)=f(n-1)$ when $3$ does not divide $n$, and $f(n)=f(n-1)+f\left(\frac{n}{3}\right)$ when $3$ divides $n$. So $f$ changes only at multiples of $3$. Building the table gives $f(9)=5$ and $f(27)=23$, and just one more multiple of $3$ remains.
solution:
Let $f(n)$ be the number of sequences from $1$ to $n$. Every key press strictly increases the display, so $f(1)=1$. For $n\ge2$, split by the last press: "add $1$" contributes $f(n-1)$, and "multiply by $3$" contributes $f(n/3)$ when $3\mid n$. Hence $f(n)=f(n-1)$ if $3\nmid n$, and $f(n)=f(n-1)+f(n/3)$ if $3\mid n$.

So $f(2)=1$, and
$$f(3)=1+1=2,\ f(6)=2+f(2)=3,\ f(9)=3+f(3)=5,\ f(12)=5+f(4)=5+2=7,\ f(15)=7+f(5)=9,$$
$$f(18)=9+f(6)=12,\ f(21)=12+f(7)=12+3=15,\ f(24)=15+f(8)=18,\ f(27)=18+f(9)=23,\ f(30)=23+f(10)=23+5=28.$$

Here $f(4)=f(5)=f(3)$, $f(7)=f(8)=f(6)$ and $f(10)=f(9)$ were used.
